The proposed answer of 1 is plausible, but I am recalling the supporting result rather than proving it, and the written argument is only a sketch.

**What the argument gets right.** The inclusion $S_k(\Gamma_1(\mathfrak{n}\wp)) \subset S_k(\Gamma_1(\mathfrak{n}\wp^r))$ is valid, so every eigensystem $\lambda$ at level $\mathfrak{n}\wp$ also appears at level $\mathfrak{n}\wp^r$. Finite slope means the $U_\wp$-eigenvalue is nonzero.

**The classical analogue.** For an oldform coming from level $N$, the old space at level $Np^r$ is spanned by $f(p^i z)$ for $0 \le i \le r$. On this space $U_p$ has the two nonzero eigenvalues $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and the eigenvalue $0$ with multiplicity $r-1$. The nonzero part therefore does not grow with $r$. This is why the multiplicity of a finite-slope eigensystem is independent of $r$.

**The Drinfeld case.** I recall a result that the multiplicity of a finite-slope eigensystem is independent of the power of $\wp$ in the level, which would give ratio 1. I did not re-derive it here. The local claim in the proposed solution, that the $\alpha$-eigenspace of $U_\wp$ is one-dimensional on $\pi_\wp^{K_1(\wp^r)}$ for all $r \ge 1$, is asserted rather than proved, and the "newform vector" label is loose. The conclusion still matches the classical picture and my recollection.

VERDICT: ACCEPT
